rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods - one-season (winter 2024-25) RBD field trial on four-year-old guava at Baruipur, West Bengal, eight treatments (SMS vs no SMS x flood/furrow/sprinkler/drip), three replications, capacitive sensor installed and calibrated. Q2: Table 1 and Table 2 / Results - SMS reduced seasonal water applied irrespective of method (e.g. flood 17965 l/plot without SMS vs 11396 l with SMS; drip 9060 vs 3337 l), irrigation efficiency rose from 25.10% (flood, no SMS) to 89.94% (drip + SMS), water saving 28-63% with SMS. Q4: Table 1 / Fig. 1 - the study measured the intermediate pathway: SMS widened irrigation intervals (15.33 to 19.67 days for flood) and reduced number of irrigations, plus conveyance and field application efficiency components in Table 2. Q9: Tables 1 and 2 report SEM and CD(0.05) for water amount per irrigation, interval, frequency, water irrigated and the three efficiency measures.
rows.notes: Single site, single crop, single soil, single season, 20 m2 plots. Water saving is derived from the one measurement of water applied (no second independent method). No limitations stated; no conditions for the effect stated as requirements (canal type mentioned as affecting losses but not as a condition). Irrigation was applied manually from sensor readings, not automated. Q4 given with some doubt: interval/frequency are components of the applied water total rather than a separately measured soil-water variable.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods - own field trial on guava with eight treatments and three replications.
rows.notes: The study tests a capacitive soil moisture sensor with manual irrigation based on sensor readings; there is no app, software scheduling tool, IoT architecture, or layered decision system. It shows SMS-guided irrigation reduced applied water and raised irrigation efficiency (Tables 1-2), but provides no evidence on app-based scheduling.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods - one-season RBD field trial on guava with SMS vs no-SMS under four irrigation methods, three replications. Q2: Tables 1-2 / Results - sensor-guided irrigation cut seasonal water applied for every method and raised irrigation efficiency (up to 89.94% for drip + SMS vs 25.10% flood without SMS), with 28-63% water saving. Q4: Table 1 / Fig. 1 - intervals widened and irrigation frequency fell when the sensor determined timing, plus conveyance and field application efficiency components (Table 2). Q9: Tables 1 and 2 give SEM and CD(0.05) for applied water and efficiency measures.
rows.notes: Only the soil-sensor/efficiency part of the passage is supported; the study has no IoT architecture, no layered approach and no measure of operational delays or user complexity (irrigation applied manually from sensor readings). Single site, crop, soil and season; 20 m2 plots; one measurement method; no limitations or stated conditions.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods - own field trial on guava with eight treatments and three replications.
rows.notes: The study reports water applied, irrigation efficiency, fruit quality/yield and B:C ratio for sensor-guided irrigation; it does not measure resilience, risk reduction, drought or stress buffering, or any system robustness outcome. Water saving is at most a precondition of the claimed resilience effect. No IoT architecture or layered approach was tested.

notes: Short original research article; full text appears complete. Single-season, single-site plot trial with a calibrated capacitive soil moisture sensor and manual irrigation; no IoT, app or automation component. Abstract and results text contain an inconsistency (5.53 vs 553 times) but this does not affect the ratings.
